samples.summary: Cross-provider account merge keyed on email equality alone, with no explicit linking confirmation — adding Google makes every GitHub-created account reachable by whoever holds a Google account with the same address
samples.evidence:
`findOrCreateUser` (packages/backend/src/user/user.service.ts:128-148) looks the user up by `email` only. Line 135 (`if (user.emailVerifiedAt) return user;`) returns — and `AuthController.finishWebLogin` (auth.controller.ts:355) then mints access+refresh session cookies for — an existing row whose `authProvider` is *different* from the one that just authenticated, with no confirmation from an already-authenticated session. Before this change only GitHub could reach a row; now a Google sign-in can. The `emailVerifiedAt` gate only covers rows that are still NULL: any row created after this change (createUserWithWorkspace stamps `new Date()` unconditionally, line 180) or re-stamped by one same-provider sign-in (line 141-144) is merged into unconditionally forever after.

Attack shape: obtain a Google account whose `email_verified` address equals a victim's Wafflebase email, sign in at `/auth/google`, and receive a session for the victim's account and workspace. That is reachable without compromising GitHub whenever the two providers' verification standards diverge — e.g. a Google Workspace domain whose owner can mint any local-part at will, a corporate/alias address later reassigned to a new employee, or a domain that changed hands after the victim verified it on GitHub. `GoogleStrategy.validate` checks only `email_verified` / `verified_email` (google.strategy.ts:59-64); it does not consult the `hd` claim, so a Workspace-issued address is indistinguishable from a personal gmail.com one.

OAuth 2.0 security BCP and the usual account-linking guidance call for the link to be confirmed from an authenticated session rather than inferred from email equality. The design docs (docs/design/backend.md 'Provider identity is the email address') record this as a deliberate decision, and `Out of scope` in the task doc says there is no linking UI — so nothing in the change blocks it. Flagging because the blast radius (full session + workspace access) is takeover-grade and the decision is now load-bearing on a third party's verification semantics.

samples.summary: `oauthRefusal` fails open: a strategy refusal carrying any code outside the three-entry allowlist is treated as a valid profile and flows into `findOrCreateUser`
samples.evidence:
`resolveOAuthUser` decides whether a passport result is a refusal purely by `oauthRefusal(profile)` (auth.controller.ts:260), which returns `undefined` unless `profile.error` is exactly one of `OAUTH_REFUSAL_CODES` (auth.types.ts:47-53). Any other truthy `error` value on the object falls through to line 265, where `profile.username!` / `profile.email!` — both absent on an `OAuthRefusal` — are passed to `findOrCreateUser`. The refusal object is thereby re-interpreted as a sign-in.

The safe direction here is the opposite one: the decision should be 'this is a profile only if it has a verified email and no error field', not 'this is a refusal only if its error string is on a list'. Today both strategies only emit listed codes, so the chain stops at a Prisma validation error on `where: { email: undefined }` (a 500, no session) rather than a session — which is why confidence is low. But the allowlist is the *only* thing standing between a refusal and a session issue, it lives in a different file from the two producers, and a third provider or a renamed code silently turns a refusal into a sign-in attempt. Severity is set by impact if the fail-open ever reaches `findOrCreateUser` with an attacker-supplied email.

samples.summary: The email-verification check — the load-bearing gate for cross-provider merge — accepts the loose string `"true"` (any case, any surrounding whitespace) as well as boolean `true`
samples.evidence: `isVerifiedFlag` (google.strategy.ts:21-23) and the identical `isFlagSet` (github.strategy.ts:29-31) return true for `value === true` OR for any string whose trimmed lowercase form is `"true"`. This is the single check that decides whether an address may be merged into an existing account (`findOrCreateUser` matches on email alone), so widening it from a strict boolean comparison widens the authentication boundary itself. The justification in the comment (Google's userinfo has historically returned the string) is real, but the same helper is applied to `emails[].verified` and to *both* `email_verified` and `verified_email` raw claims, and on the GitHub side to `verified`/`primary` from `GET /user/emails`, where the API contract is a JSON boolean and no string form has ever been observed. A strict boolean check on the GitHub side, with the loose form confined to the one Google claim that needs it, keeps the widening off the path that does not. Not exploitable as written (the value comes from a server-to-server response), which is why this is minor rather than higher.

samples.summary: The browser OAuth `state` is not bound to the provider that minted it — one cookie name and one opaque token serve both `/auth/github` and `/auth/google`
samples.evidence:
`startWebOAuthLogin` (web-oauth-login.ts:42-51) mints `createWebOAuthState()` into the single cookie `oauthStateCookieName()` ('wafflebase_oauth_state') for both providers, and `consumeWebOAuthState` (line 63-75) compares only `state === 'web.' + sha256(cookie)` with no provider tag. Consequently a `state` minted by `GET /auth/google` is, by construction, accepted at `GET /auth/github/callback` (auth.controller.ts:157) and vice versa (auth.controller.ts:324). A provider-scoped value (e.g. `web.github.<hash>` / a per-provider cookie name, or hashing the provider into the token) would make the two vocabularies non-interchangeable at no cost.

I could not complete an exploit chain: redeeming a state at the other provider's callback additionally requires an authorization code that provider's passport strategy will accept, and the state value itself never leaves the victim's browser toward an attacker-readable origin (it travels only to accounts.google.com / github.com). So this is reported as missing defence-in-depth around a mixed-provider replay, not a demonstrated bypass. Searched: web-oauth-login.ts, oauth-state.ts (createWebOAuthState/isWebOAuthState/webOAuthStateMatches), github-auth.guard.ts, google-auth.guard.ts, auth.controller.ts callbacks, and grepped `AuthGuard(` across packages/backend/src for other consumers of this cookie.

samples.summary: GitHub sign-in identity now silently falls back to an arbitrary non-primary verified address, making the account key depend on GitHub's list ordering rather than on a stable, user-visible choice
samples.evidence: `verifiedEmail` (github.strategy.ts:58-65) picks the primary verified address, else `verified[0]` — the first verified row in whatever order `GET /user/emails` happens to return. That value is the whole account identity: it is what `findOrCreateUser` matches on (user.service.ts:129-133) and, on a first sight, what a new row is created under. Two security-relevant consequences: (a) a user whose primary is unverified is now signed into a *different* account than before this change, and the row keyed on their old unverified primary is left orphaned with `emailVerifiedAt: null`, permanently unclaimable by anyone (cross-provider merge into it is refused at user.service.ts:136-138); (b) the identity a session is issued for can change between two logins of the same GitHub account without the user doing anything, purely because GitHub reordered or the user re-flagged addresses. An identity that is not stable across logins is a weak basis for the email-keyed merge in the previous finding. A deterministic rule (refuse outright when the primary is unverified, or sort the candidates) would remove the ordering dependence.

verdict.reason: The code is present exactly as described and no guard blocks it. `findOrCreateUser` (user.service.ts:128-133) matches on email alone; line 135 `if (user.emailVerifiedAt) return user;` short-circuits before the `authProvider` comparison, so the `EmailProviderConflictError` at lines 136-138 protects only rows whose `emailVerifiedAt` is still NULL. `createUserWithWorkspace` stamps `emailVerifiedAt: data.emailVerifiedAt ?? new Date()` unconditionally (line 180), and lines 141-144 re-stamp legacy rows after one same-provider sign-in, so the mergeable population grows monotonically and the conflict guard becomes permanently unreachable for those rows. `auth.controller.ts:338-343` passes the resolved row into `finishWebLogin` (line 355-357), which mints access+refresh cookies — a full session on an account created under a different provider, with no confirmation from an already-authenticated session. `GoogleStrategy.resolveEmail` (google.strategy.ts:50-65) checks only `email_verified`/`verified_email` and never the `hd` claim, so a Google Workspace address whose domain admin can mint arbitrary local parts is indistinguishable from a personal one; that is the concrete vector for reaching a GitHub-created victim row. docs/design/backend.md:921-947 records this as deliberate and confirms there is no account-linking UI, i.e. nothing supplies the missing explicit-link step. Refutation grounds do not apply: the code is present (not `not-present`), the emailVerifiedAt check does not cover the described path (not `already-guarded`), and cross-provider account linking plus session issuance is core authorization/auth (not `out-of-scope`). Impact is takeover-grade, so it stands as blocking under the security rubric.

verdict.reason: The described code exists (auth.types.ts:47-53 allowlist; auth.controller.ts:260-270 non-refusal fallthrough), but the fail-open branch is unreachable. The only producers of the `req.user` value reaching `resolveOAuthUser` are GitHubStrategy.validate and GoogleStrategy.validate, both declared to return `... | OAuthRefusal` (github.strategy.ts:129, google.strategy.ts:114) where `OAuthRefusal.error` is typed `OAuthRefusalCode` (auth.types.ts:33-36). The only refusal literals emitted are `'unverified_email'` (github.strategy.ts:145, google.strategy.ts:129) and `'no_email'` (google.strategy.ts:125) — all on the allowlist. Their success paths (github.strategy.ts:148-155, google.strategy.ts:132-139) build fresh object literals that never spread the provider profile, so no provider- or attacker-controlled `error` field can ride along. `email_conflict` is not strategy-produced at all; it is synthesized in the controller catch (auth.controller.ts:273). All three call sites (auth.controller.ts:165, 218, 338) take `req.user` from AuthGuard('github')/AuthGuard('google') only (github-auth.guard.ts:192, google-auth.guard.ts:37,55). No attacker-reachable input yields an unlisted truthy `error`, and the reviewer concedes the chain stops today; the remaining argument is defensive design against a hypothetical future provider, which is a robustness/hardening preference rather than a present authorization, injection, or crypto defect in the security lane.

finding.summary: Cross-provider email merge is switched on with no cleanup of User rows already created from unverified GitHub emails
finding.evidence:
This PR makes the email address the shared identity across two providers: `googleAuthCallback` (auth.controller.ts:280) calls the same `findOrCreateUser`, which matches on `email` alone (`prisma.user.findUnique({ where: { email: data.email } })`, user.service.ts:41-45). The PR's own rationale (github.strategy.ts:43-47, docs/design/backend.md risk entry) states that before this change GitHub's primary address was taken without reading its `verified` flag, and that an unverified address can be the primary. So rows keyed on an address the holder never proved ownership of may already exist in any deployment.

Attack: Mallory signed in with GitHub at any point before this change while `victim@corp.com` sat as her primary, unverified address — auth.controller.ts (pre-change `email: emails?.[0]?.value`) created a User row keyed on it and gave her a session. After this PR ships, the real owner of `victim@corp.com` clicks "Continue with Google"; `GoogleStrategy.validate` correctly confirms Google verified the address, and `findOrCreateUser` then resolves it to Mallory's *existing* row rather than creating one. The victim and Mallory are now the same user: Mallory's outstanding access/refresh cookies (7-day refresh, auth.controller.ts:46) authenticate as the victim and see every workspace, document and datasource the victim creates.

The forward path is closed (`verifiedEmail` at github.strategy.ts:57-64 now refuses), but nothing addresses the backfill: there is no `emailVerified` column on `User` (prisma/schema.prisma), and no migration in this change or any prior one touches the users table for this (I listed all 23 files under packages/backend/prisma/migrations/). There is therefore no way for an operator to tell which existing rows are safe to merge into, and no re-verification step on first cross-provider sign-in.

verdict.reason: The finding claims there is no `emailVerified` column on User, no migration touching the users table, and no re-verification step guarding cross-provider merge into rows created from unverified GitHub emails. All three are present in the working tree. `prisma/schema.prisma:12` declares `emailVerifiedAt DateTime?`; migration `20260915120000_add_user_email_verified_at/migration.sql:6` adds the column with an explicit comment that it is intentionally NULL for legacy rows because a GitHub primary address may be unverified; and `user.service.ts:134-145` refuses (throws `EmailProviderConflictError`, defined at :14-23) any cross-provider sign-in that resolves to a row whose `emailVerifiedAt` is null, only merging after the originating provider re-proves the address (:141-144). The reviewer's exact attack is blocked: Mallory's legacy GitHub row for victim@corp.com has emailVerifiedAt NULL, so the victim's Google sign-in hits `user.authProvider !== data.authProvider` and is refused rather than merged. The refusal reaches the enforced path — the sole non-test caller `AuthController.resolveOAuthUser` (auth.controller.ts:265) converts it to `error: 'email_conflict'` (:272-273), consumed by googleAuthCallback (:338-341), auth.types.ts:27, frontend login-form.tsx:48 and cli login.ts:605. New rows are stamped verified at creation (user.service.ts:180), so only legacy rows are in the unproven set. Tests at user.service.spec.ts:187-192 / :231-234 and auth.controller.spec.ts:696-715 pin the behaviour. The reviewer's migration enumeration missed this 24th migration file.
